headline: Agreed to edits to syringe litter report, including removing Howard Center references.
summary: Residents submitted public comment opposing proposed zoning Section 4.04, which could affect syringe service programs. City Council President Ben Traverse presented revised Burlington Forward resolution language. The meeting agreed to edits to the syringe litter report.
decisions: Agreed to edits to the syringe litter report, including removing references to the Howard Center and refining SeeClickFix recommendations.

decision_evidence.quote: Committee members went through each recommendation in the report and incorporated LSP's edits. They agreed to remove references to the Howard Center, clarify the role of state agencies and service providers in harm reduction, and refine recommendations regarding the use of SeeClickFix for reporting syringe litter.

Other Attendees:  City Council President Ben Traverse, Chris McGrath, Ed Baker, Bella Fearn 
 
Draft Minutes 
 
Meeting Started at 6:02 PM 
 
1. Approve agenda   
MOTION by Councilor Schachter, SECOND by Councilor Sanchez-Parkinson, 
to approve the agenda 
VOTING: unanimous; motion carries. 
 
2. Adopt Minutes   
MOTION by Councilor Sanchez-Parkinson, SECOND by Councilor Litwin, to 
approve the 10/6/26 minutes 
VOTING: unanimous; motion carries. 
 
 
 
CITY OF BURLINGTON, VERMONT 
CITY COUNCIL COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT & 
NEIGHBORHOOD REVITALIZATION COMMITTEE 
c/o Community & Economic Development Office 
City Hall, Room 32 • 149 Church Street • Burlington, VT 05401 
802-865-7144 VOX • 802-865-7024 FAX • www.burlingtonvt.gov/cedo
3. Public Forum  
• Bella Fearn submitted the following for public comment: "I am 
concerned that Section 4.04 could lead to zoning restrictions that displace 
or eliminate syringe service programs. This would likely lead to increased 
syringe litter, raise the risk of hepatitis C and HIV transmission, increase 
overdose death, remove on-ramps to treatment, eliminate services that 
help people obtain and maintain stable housing, and increase public drug 
use. Syringe service programs are about much more than distributing 
sterile supplies. They connect people to treatment, medications for opioid 
use disorder (MOUD), mental health care, housing assistance, 
transportation to appointments, and other support services. They also 
help prevent the spread of infectious diseases, including hepatitis C, by 
providing sterile equipment and other harm reduction services. These 
programs are often a critical point of connection for people who do not 
access traditional recovery services. They build trust, help people navigate 
available resources, and create opportunities to help people make 
informed decisions about their health. Additionally, When syringe service 
programs close or become less accessible, people have fewer 
opportunities to obtain sterile supplies and safely dispose of used syringes. 
Research from other communities has shown that closing these programs 
does not eliminate substance use. It can instead make it harder to manage 
its public health impacts, including safe syringe disposal. If the City wants 
to address syringe litter and improve public spaces, it should work with 
existing service providers and the people who use these services to expand 
access to safe disposal, strengthen outreach, and develop practical 
solutions. Restricting access to services without a clear, accessible 
alternative risks making the problems this resolution seeks to address 
more difficult to manage. Burlington can address concerns about public 
spaces while continuing to support harm reduction and access to health 
care. These goals do not have to be in conflict.  I urge the City Council to 
reconsider the proposed restrictions in Section 4.04 and prioritize 
collaboration with public health providers, community members, and 
people with lived experience to develop solutions that protect both public 
health and the broader community. I would also ask at a minimum that the 
city council pause in order to seek expert provider and researcher 
perspectives on this issue. This section has the ability to cause significant 
harm to already very vulnerable people and is likely to make public 
impacts related to substance use and syringe disposal much worse. With 
all this in mind, I think it makes a lot of sense to draw on expert opinions 
before making decisions of this magnitude."
• Ed Baker shared data from New York City’s overdose prevention 
center to highlight its impact on hazardous waste collection and cost 
savings. 
 
4. Q&A with City Council President Ben Traverse re: Burlington Forward next 
steps 
o President Traverse presented the revised Burlington Forward 
resolution, which included new language on a community 
stabilization and diversion center, public safety response teams, and 
a prohibition on automatic license plate readers. He also clarified 
that the resolution’s zoning language regarding an overdose 
prevention center applied specifically to the downtown improvement 
district. 
 
5. Syringe Litter Report 
• Committee members went through each recommendation in the 
report and incorporated LSP’s edits. They agreed to remove 
references to the Howard Center, clarify the role of state agencies 
and service providers in harm reduction, and refine 
recommendations regarding the use of SeeClickFix for reporting 
syringe litter. The committee also discussed the need for clarity from 
the Vermont Department of Health on how a future overdose 
prevention center would impact existing syringe service programs. 
 
6. Adjournment   
• ADJOURN at 8:20 p.m. by Councilor Litwin with no objection
